parole.significato: stud (a ranch where horses are kept)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian barem or Bulgarian барем (barem), from Ottoman Turkish باری (bari), from Persian باری (bâri).
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian basna. Doublet of basm.

parole.significato: a rounded white pebble found in the rivers

parole.testo: Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian birt, from German Wirt.

parole.significato: a type of bean, field bean, horse bean, broad bean

parole.testo: Cf. boș, olog. Possibly influenced by Serbo-Croatian bosonog.
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian burma, from Ottoman Turkish بورمه (burma), from بورمق (burmak, “to twist”).
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian bòsiljak or Hungarian bosziók, busziók; cf. also Bulgarian босилек (bosilek), Albanian borzilok. Ultimately derived from Ancient Greek βασιλικόν (basilikón).
Probably formed from a compound of several Slavic words like Serbo-Croatian bazdrk, Russian бздёх (bzdjox), and dâcă. Alternative, from Turkish bızdık, (“child”, “tot”, or as a slang “ass”).
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian četnik, from četa (“band, group”) + -nik, from Proto-Slavic *četa.
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian kirija, borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كرا (kira), borrowed from Arabic كِرَاء (kirāʔ).
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian kititi, from Proto-Slavic *kytiti.
Borrowed, through metathesis, from Serbo-Croatian печурка (pečurka, “mushroom”) or Bulgarian печурка (pečurka), from Proto-Slavic *pečura.
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian kočija or Hungarian kocsi.
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian kocka, from Proto-Slavic *kostъka (“small bone”).
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian krov, from Proto-Slavic *krovъ.
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian krumpir, from Bavarian grumper, krumbeer, from Alemannic German Grumbeer, compound of Grund (“ground”) + Beer (“pear”).
Probably from Serbo-Croatian kukùmar, from Venetan cucùmaro, from Latin cucumis, cucumerem.
Unknown. Possibly from Serbo-Croatian kukurek or Bulgarian кукурег (kukureg, “fragrant hellebore”), кукуряг (kukurjag), but they could also come from Romanian.
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian kamuka or Hungarian kamuka.
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian dolina, from Proto-Slavic *dolъ + *-ina.

parole.significato: a traditional dish usually served at Easter made from minced up offal and entrails (often of lamb), seasoned with herbs…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian drob or Bulgarian дроб (drob), from Proto-Slavic *drobъ (“entrails”). Doublet of dărab.
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian duhan, from Ottoman Turkish دخان, from Arabic دُخَان (duḵān).

Uncertain. Possibilities include: * Scriban argues that the term is related to grăunte or grunț, both meaning “grain; kernel”. * Per Skok, the term is from borrowed from Serbo-Croatian glonta (“bullet”), which he derives from German Flinte (“little rifle”). * Per Cihac, the term is borrowed from Hun

parole.significato: a heap of soil or stones used as a marker to delineate a border

parole.testo: Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian gusle or French guzla.
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian јоргован, from Ottoman Turkish ارغوان (ergavan, erguvan), from Persian ارغوان (arġavân, arġuvân, “purple; Judas tree”), from Akkadian 𒅈𒂵𒌋𒌋𒉡 (argamannu).

neck yoke to prevent animals from jumping over fences
a loaf of round wheaten yeast bread, pita
parole.testo: Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian lepinja, from Hungarian lepény

parole.significato: scoop, peel (used to remove bread from an oven)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian lubenica or Bulgarian любеница (ljubenica).
Variant of vlăstar. From Serbo-Croatian lastar.
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian međaš or Hungarian megyés.
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian mrmoljak, from Ancient Greek μορμολύκειον (mormolúkeion), a cognate of Μορμώ (Mormṓ).
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian mučenje or Russian мучение (mučenije).
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian ogar or Hungarian agár, from Old Hungarian agar, from a West Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *ogarь.
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian pandur or Hungarian pandúr.
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian perina, from Proto-Slavic *perina.
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian pogača or Hungarian pogácsa or German Pogatsche. Doublet of focaccia.
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian postava or Bulgarian постав (postav).
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian prepelica or Bulgarian препелица (prepelica), from Proto-Slavic *perpelъ.
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian prsnuti or Bulgarian пръсна (prăsna). Compare Russian прыскать (pryskatʹ). The noun is denominated from the verb. Doublet of împroșca. First attested in 1830.

Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian skela (“scaffolding”) or Bulgarian скеля (skelja), from Ottoman Turkish اسكله (iskele, “scaffolding”), from Italian scala (“ladder”), from Latin scala. Doublet of scală, escală, and scară.
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian smotka, influenced by smâc.
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian sokak, from Ottoman Turkish سوقاق (sokak), from Persian زقاق (zoqâq), from Arabic زُقَاق (zuqāq).
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian steglić, Bulgarian щиглец (štiglec), from Proto-Slavic *ščigъlъ, *ščegъlъ.
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian stradalnik, from stradati (“to suffer”), from Proto-Slavic *stradati (“to suffer”).
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian srb, Srbin or Bulgarian съ́рбин (sắrbin), from Proto-Slavic *sьrbъ.
Unknown. Probably borrowed from Serbo-Croatian tur. Other less likely theories suggest a link with stur, or Latin thylacus, from Ancient Greek θύλακος (thúlakos).
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian троносати, from Old Church Slavonic троносъ (tronosŭ, “throne”), from Ancient Greek θρόνος (thrónos).

parole.significato: member of the Ustashe fascist movement

parole.testo: Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian zavera or Bulgarian завера (zavera).

parole.significato: to dry or air (out in the sun or wind)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian glomot, borrowed from Polish gomon. Compare Russian загомонить (zagomonitʹ, “to start chattering, to start talking loudly”).

From șindră + -ilă, from Serbo-Croatian šindra, from German Schindel, itself from Middle High German schindel, from Old High German scintula, from Proto-West Germanic *skindulā, from Late Latin scindula, from Latin scandula. Compare Hungarian zsindely. Doublet of scândură.

Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian šljivovica, from šljȉva (“plum”), from Proto-Slavic *sliva (“plum”). Compare Polish śliwowica, Czech slivovice, German Slibowitz, Hungarian sligovica, Russian сливовица (slivovica).
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian šuba or Hungarian suba, from Middle High German schūbe, from Italian giubba, from Arabic جُبَّة (jubba, “long garment”). Doublet of jupă and giubea.

parole.significato: to lose one's mind, to become insane

parole.testo: Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian cigla, from German Ziegel, from Latin tegula.
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian cincar, from Aromanian tsintsi.
